title: Singapore's 2026 Government Bond Auction Schedule – A Quick Overview
abstract: Singapore's 2026 government bond auction calendar is out, and the rewrite desk has the breezy rundown on what's on tap.
body:
## The 2026 Auction Calendar Is Here

Singapore's government bond auction schedule for 2026 has landed, and the rewrite desk is here to give you the breezy rundown. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) released the calendar on 10 April 2026, laying out a full year of Singapore Government Securities (SGS) auctions. If you're a fixed-income watcher, this is your roadmap for the year ahead. The schedule includes a mix of short-term Treasury bills and longer-dated bonds, with a few new issues and some reopenings of existing lines. MAS says the issuance programme is designed to meet the government's borrowing needs and support the development of the domestic bond market. Nothing too surprising, but plenty to keep an eye on.

## T-Bills and Bonds on the Menu

Let's break it down. The 2026 calendar features 24 auctions of 6-month T-bills and 12 auctions of 1-year T-bills, sticking to the usual monthly and bi-monthly rhythms. On the bond side, there are four new 2-year SGS issues, four new 5-year SGS issues, and two new 10-year SGS issues. MAS also plans to reopen existing 2-year, 5-year, and 10-year benchmarks to maintain liquidity. The total gross issuance for 2026 is projected at S$45 billion, a slight uptick from 2025's S$43 billion. That's a modest increase, reflecting the government's continued funding needs and the maturity of some older bonds. The first auction of the year is a 6-month T-bill on 14 January 2026, so mark your calendars.

## Key Dates and What to Watch

A few dates stand out. The first new 2-year SGS auction is scheduled for 3 February 2026, followed by the first new 5-year on 17 March 2026. The first new 10-year SGS will hit the market on 5 May 2026. MAS has also pencilled in a 30-year SGS reopening on 7 July 2026, which should attract long-duration buyers. The auction sizes will vary, with T-bill auctions typically ranging from S$3 billion to S$4 billion, while bond auctions are expected to be between S$2.5 billion and S$3.5 billion. MAS notes that it will adjust auction sizes based on market conditions and demand. The full schedule is available on the MAS website, so if you need the nitty-gritty, head there.

## Why This Matters for Investors

For investors, the 2026 auction calendar provides clarity on supply, which can influence yields and trading strategies. The steady pace of issuance should help keep the SGS market liquid and deep, which is good news for both local and foreign investors. The slight increase in gross issuance might put some upward pressure on yields, but MAS's careful calibration should prevent any major disruptions. It's also worth noting that the 30-year reopening will be a key event for pension funds and insurers looking to match long-term liabilities. Overall, the calendar is a useful tool for anyone planning their fixed-income allocations for the year. Keep an eye on MAS announcements for any changes, as the authority retains the flexibility to tweak the schedule if needed.

## The Global Backdrop

The 2026 auction schedule comes amid a shifting global interest rate environment. The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is expected to continue its gradual policy normalisation, while the US Federal Reserve's path remains data-dependent. In this context, Singapore's stable issuance plan offers a predictable option for yield-seeking investors. MAS has reiterated that its primary objective is to ensure orderly market conditions, not to target a specific yield level. The SGS market remains a safe-haven asset in the region, and the 2026 calendar reinforces that status. For those keeping score, the next update from MAS on auction results will be after the first T-bill auction in January. Until then, the calendar is your best guide.

## Wrapping It Up

So there you have it: Singapore's 2026 government bond auction schedule is set, with a steady stream of T-bills and bonds to keep the market humming. The modest increase in issuance reflects the government's funding needs without rocking the boat. Key dates include the first 2-year SGS on 3 February 2026 and the first 10-year on 5 May 2026, with a 30-year reopening on 7 July 2026. Investors should mark these dates and watch for any adjustments from MAS. As always, the rewrite desk will be here to summarise the results and any market impact. Stay tuned.
